title: Two Sum
notes:
Task and constraints: The array has at least two integers and exactly one pair sums to target. Values can be negative, so lookup must use the actual complement.
Idea: Scan left to right, storing earlier values and their indices. For each value, look for target minus that value before inserting the current value.
Technique and why it applies: A hash map provides expected constant-time complement lookup, avoiding the quadratic search through every pair.
Invariant: Before index i is processed, the map contains only values from indices less than i. Any match therefore uses a distinct earlier element.
Edge cases: Negative values and duplicate values are valid. Checking before insertion prevents using the same index twice; the problem guarantees a match.
Complexity: Time is O(n) expected because each value causes one lookup and insertion. Extra space is O(n) because the map can hold all processed elements.
complexity_reason: One pass with expected constant-time hash operations; map stores up to n values.

title: Add Two Numbers
notes:
Task and constraints: Two linked lists store non-negative integers in reverse digit order. Each list has 1 to 100 nodes, with digits from 0 through 9.
Idea: Add available digits and carry, appending each result digit to a new list. Continue while either list has nodes or carry remains.
Technique and why it applies: Ordinary decimal column addition follows the same order as the least-significant-first list representation and avoids converting long numbers into a machine integer.
Invariant: The result list contains the correct sum digits for all processed positions; carry is the amount to add at the next position.
Edge cases: Lists may have different lengths, and the final addition may produce an extra carry node. ListNode is supplied by the judge.
Complexity: Time is O(max(m,n)) because each input node is visited once. Extra space is O(max(m,n)) for the newly allocated result nodes.
code:
from typing import Optional

class Solution:
    def addTwoNumbers(self, l1: Optional[ListNode], l2: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        dummy = ListNode(0)
        tail = dummy
        carry = 0
        while l1 or l2 or carry:
            total = carry
            if l1:
                total += l1.val
                l1 = l1.next
            if l2:
                total += l2.val
                l2 = l2.next
            carry, digit = divmod(total, 10)
            tail.next = ListNode(digit)
            tail = tail.next
        return dummy.next
complexity_reason: Each input node is visited once and one result node is allocated per output digit.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
notes:
Task and constraints: The input string has length up to 50,000. Find the maximum length of a contiguous substring containing distinct characters.
Idea: Maintain a window and each character's latest index. When a repeated character occurs inside the window, move the left boundary just past its previous occurrence.
Technique and why it applies: The right boundary advances once and the left boundary never moves backward. Last-seen indices restore validity without shrinking one step at a time.
Invariant: After adjusting the left boundary at each right index, the current window contains no repeated characters; its length is therefore a valid candidate.
Edge cases: An empty string returns zero. An old occurrence before the current window must not move the left boundary backward.
Complexity: Time is O(n) expected with constant-expected-time map operations per character. Space is O(min(n, alphabet)) for stored character indices.
complexity_reason: Each character is processed once; the map records the latest index of each encountered character.

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
notes:
Task and constraints: Two sorted arrays have combined length at least one; either array may be empty. The requested logarithmic time rules out merging every element.
Idea: Binary-search a cut in the shorter array and derive the matching cut in the longer array so the left side contains half the values.
Technique and why it applies: Sorted order means the correct partition is characterized by four boundary values; moving the cut fixes a crossed boundary in logarithmic time.
Invariant: The search maintains candidate cuts in the shorter array; a valid cut has each left boundary no greater than the opposite right boundary.
Edge cases: Handle empty sides and partitions at either array end with infinities. For even total length, average the two middle boundary values using floating-point division.
Complexity: Time is O(log(min(m,n))) due to binary search. Extra space is O(1) because only indices and boundary values are stored.
complexity_reason: Binary search over the shorter array; only a constant number of boundary values are stored.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
notes:
Task and constraints: The input is a non-empty string of at most 1,000 letters and digits; return a longest palindromic substring, not merely its length.
Idea: Treat each character and each gap between characters as a possible palindrome center, expanding while the two sides match.
Technique and why it applies: Every palindrome has either one middle character or one middle gap, so checking both center types covers all candidates without storing a DP table.
Invariant: During each expansion, the examined interval remains a palindrome because its outer characters match and the inner interval was already a palindrome.
Edge cases: A single character returns itself. Even-length palindromes need gap centers; ties may return any longest answer, as allowed.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2) in the worst case because each center may expand across the string. Extra space is O(1) beyond the returned substring.
complexity_reason: There are 2n-1 centers, each expanding at most O(n); only indices are maintained.

title: Zigzag Conversion
notes:
Task and constraints: The string contains 1 to 1,000 permitted characters and numRows is between 1 and 1,000. Output is the row-by-row reading of the zigzag arrangement.
Idea: Keep one character buffer per row and append each input character to the current row, reversing direction at the top and bottom rows.
Technique and why it applies: The zigzag's row sequence is deterministic; storing rows directly avoids allocating a mostly empty rectangular grid.
Invariant: After processing a prefix of s, each row buffer contains exactly the characters from that prefix that belong to that row, in original order.
Edge cases: When numRows is one or at least the string length, the result is unchanged. Direction reversal must happen before advancing away from a boundary.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each character is appended once and rows are joined once. Space is O(n) for row buffers and output.
complexity_reason: Each character is stored in exactly one row buffer and then included in the output.

title: Reverse Integer
notes:
Task and constraints: Reverse the digits of a signed 32-bit integer and return zero if the result falls outside the signed 32-bit range.
Idea: Repeatedly remove the last decimal digit and append it to a reversed accumulator, then check the final value against the allowed bounds.
Technique and why it applies: Decimal remainder and division expose digits without building a full reversed string. A wider temporary integer lets Java detect overflow before narrowing to int.
Invariant: After each iteration, the accumulator equals the reverse of the digits removed so far, including the original sign.
Edge cases: Trailing zeroes disappear naturally. The minimum negative integer and values whose reverse overflows must return zero.
Complexity: Time is O(log |x|) because each loop removes one digit. Extra space is O(1) because only numeric variables are stored.
space_complexity: O(log |x|) for Python string conversion; O(1) for Java arithmetic
complexity_reason: Python materializes a digit string and its reverse; Java uses a constant number of numeric variables.

title: String to Integer (atoi)
notes:
Task and constraints: Parse leading spaces, an optional sign, and the initial run of decimal digits. Return zero if no digits are found and clamp the result to the signed 32-bit range.
Idea: Move a cursor through the string, record the sign, then accumulate digits until a non-digit appears, clamping before returning.
Technique and why it applies: A single deterministic scan follows the parsing rules in order and stops at the first character that cannot extend the integer.
Invariant: After each consumed digit, the accumulator represents the magnitude of the parsed prefix, capped so the signed result cannot exceed its limit.
Edge cases: Empty input, spaces only, sign without digits, trailing words, and both positive and negative overflow must be handled.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because characters are scanned at most once. Extra space is O(1) because only indices and integer accumulators are used.
complexity_reason: The parser scans the input once and stores only scalar parsing state.

title: Palindrome Number
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether a signed 32-bit integer is a decimal palindrome. Negative numbers and nonzero values ending in zero are not palindromes.
Idea: Reject those immediate failures, then reverse only the lower half of the digits until it meets or passes the remaining half.
Technique and why it applies: Reversing half avoids a string conversion and avoids overflow from reversing the entire integer.
Invariant: The reversed accumulator contains the digits removed from the right in reverse order; the remaining value contains the left portion not yet compared.
Edge cases: Zero is a palindrome. For odd digit counts, the middle digit in the reversed half can be discarded with integer division by ten.
Complexity: Time is O(log |x|) because about half the digits are processed. Extra space is O(1) for a few integer variables.
complexity_reason: The loop handles roughly half of the decimal digits and uses constant extra variables.

title: Regular Expression Matching
notes:
Task and constraints: Match the entire input string against a pattern where dot matches one character and star repeats the preceding pattern element zero or more times. The string and pattern are small but require exact full-string matching.
Idea: Let dp[i][j] mean the first i string characters match the first j pattern characters; fill the table using ordinary matches, dot, and star transitions.
Technique and why it applies: Star can either remove its preceding atom entirely or consume one more matching character, so each state depends on smaller prefixes already computed.
Invariant: After a table cell is filled, it correctly describes whether those exact prefixes match under the pattern rules.
Edge cases: Empty string can match patterns such as a*b*. Star is handled only when j is at least two; it must never be treated as an independent character.
Complexity: Time is O(mn) for the DP table. Space is O(mn) for storing all prefix-match states.
complexity_reason: The algorithm fills (m+1) by (n+1) boolean states, each in constant time.

title: Container With Most Water
notes:
Task and constraints: The array contains at least two non-negative heights, and the area between indices i and j is their distance multiplied by the smaller height. The input can contain 100,000 values, so a quadratic scan is unsuitable.
Idea: Start with the widest pair, record its area, then move inward the pointer at the shorter line.
Technique and why it applies: The shorter line limits the current area. Moving the taller line cannot improve the limiting height and reduces width, so only moving the shorter side can reveal a better candidate.
Invariant: The maximum area seen so far is retained, and every discarded pair is dominated by a pair already considered or cannot beat the current limiting height.
Edge cases: Equal heights may move either pointer; two elements produce their only possible area. Heights may be zero.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each pointer moves inward at most n times. Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Two pointers move inward without allocating a structure.

title: Integer to Roman
notes:
Task and constraints: Convert an integer from 1 through 3999 into its standard Roman numeral representation. The representation includes subtractive pairs such as IV, IX, XL, XC, CD, and CM.
Idea: Visit values from largest to smallest, including subtractive pairs, append each symbol as many times as it fits, and subtract that value from the remaining number.
Technique and why it applies: The Roman numeral system has a fixed descending list of canonical values; greedily taking the largest available value produces the standard representation.
Invariant: After each denomination, the remaining number equals the original number minus the value represented by the output built so far.
Edge cases: Values 4, 9, 40, 90, 400, and 900 require subtractive symbols. The upper bound 3999 avoids needing a special overline notation.
Complexity: Time is O(1) under the fixed maximum of 13 denominations and bounded repetitions. Output space is O(1) under the problem's numeric limit.
complexity_reason: The denomination list is fixed and num is bounded by 3999.

title: Roman to Integer
approach_name: Subtract smaller symbols before larger ones
notes:
Task and constraints: Convert a valid Roman numeral of at most 15 characters into its integer value. Valid numerals use the standard subtractive forms and represent values from 1 through 3999.
Idea: Map each symbol to its value. If a symbol is smaller than the next symbol, subtract it; otherwise add it to the total.
Technique and why it applies: Roman notation encodes subtraction locally in pairs such as IV and CM; comparing adjacent values detects exactly those cases in a valid numeral.
Invariant: After processing a symbol, the accumulated total accounts for its contribution, except that a smaller symbol before a larger one is counted negatively.
Edge cases: The final symbol has no next symbol, so it is added. Valid input is guaranteed, so malformed sequences need not be rejected.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each symbol is examined once. Extra space is O(1) because the symbol-value map has seven entries.
complexity_reason: A fixed seven-symbol map and one pass over the input are used.

title: Longest Common Prefix
approach_name: Shrink prefix until all strings match
notes:
Task and constraints: Given one or more strings, return the longest prefix shared by all of them. Strings may be empty and the collection can contain up to 200 entries.
Idea: Scan character positions up to the shortest string length and stop at the first position where any string differs from the first string.
Technique and why it applies: Any common prefix must be a prefix of the first string, so there is no need to build a separate character-by-character result.
Invariant: Every position before the scan index has matched across all strings, so the prefix before the first mismatch is common to every string.
Edge cases: If the first string is empty, the answer is empty. If any string is empty or differs at the first character, the candidate eventually becomes empty.
Complexity: Time is O(S) in the worst case, where S is the total number of characters compared. Extra space is O(1) apart from the returned prefix.
complexity_reason: Each shortening removes a prefix character; the total compared characters is bounded by input size.

title: 3Sum
approach_name: Sort then sweep with two pointers
notes:
Task and constraints: Return every unique triplet of distinct indices whose values sum to zero. The array can contain up to 3,000 values, so cubic enumeration is too expensive.
Idea: Sort the array, fix the first value, and use left and right pointers to find pairs summing to its negation. Skip repeated values at each level.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting makes the pair sum monotonic as pointers move and places duplicates next to one another for reliable deduplication.
Invariant: For a fixed first value, all pairs outside the current pointer interval have already been considered or cannot reach the required sum by moving inward.
Edge cases: Skip duplicate first values and duplicate pair values after recording a triplet. Early stop when the fixed value becomes positive.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2) after sorting. Extra space is O(log n) typical sort stack space, excluding the output.
space_complexity: O(log n) typical sort stack, excluding output
complexity_reason: Sorting dominates the linear scan per fixed first index.
code:
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def threeSum(self, nums: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
        nums.sort()
        out = []
        n = len(nums)
        for i in range(n - 2):
            if i and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]: continue
            if nums[i] > 0: break
            left, right = i + 1, n - 1
            while left < right:
                total = nums[i] + nums[left] + nums[right]
                if total < 0: left += 1
                elif total > 0: right -= 1
                else:
                    out.append([nums[i], nums[left], nums[right]])
                    left += 1; right -= 1
                    while left < right and nums[left] == nums[left - 1]: left += 1
                    while left < right and nums[right] == nums[right + 1]: right -= 1
        return out

title: 3Sum Closest
notes:
Task and constraints: Select three distinct array elements whose sum is closest to target. There are at least three values, and exactly one sum is closest.
Idea: Sort the values, fix one index, and move two pointers according to whether the current sum is below or above target. Keep the best difference seen.
Technique and why it applies: In a sorted array, moving the left pointer raises the sum and moving the right pointer lowers it, so each step can focus on improving the target distance.
Invariant: best always stores a sum from a valid triplet with the smallest absolute target difference encountered so far.
Edge cases: Return immediately on an exact match. Initialize best from an actual three-element sum, not an arbitrary sentinel.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2) after sorting. Extra space is O(log n) typical sort stack space, excluding the input copy in Python sorting semantics.
complexity_reason: Sorting and one two-pointer sweep for each fixed index determine the time bound.
code:
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def threeSumClosest(self, nums: List[int], target: int) -> int:
        nums.sort()
        best = nums[0] + nums[1] + nums[2]
        for i in range(len(nums) - 2):
            left, right = i + 1, len(nums) - 1
            while left < right:
                total = nums[i] + nums[left] + nums[right]
                if abs(total - target) < abs(best - target): best = total
                if total == target: return total
                if total < target: left += 1
                else: right -= 1
        return best

Idea: Sort the values, fix one index, and move two pointers according to whether the current sum is below or above target. Keep the best difference seen.
Technique and why it applies: In a sorted array, moving the left pointer raises the sum and moving the right pointer lowers it, so each step can focus on improving the target distance.
Invariant: best always stores a sum from a valid triplet with the smallest absolute target difference encountered so far.
Edge cases: Return immediately on an exact match. Initialize best from an actual three-element sum, not an arbitrary sentinel.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2) after sorting. Extra space is O(log n) typical sort stack space, excluding the input copy in Python sorting semantics.
complexity_reason: Sorting and one two-pointer sweep for each fixed index determine the time bound.

title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
notes:
Task and constraints: Digits from 2 through 9 map to three or four letters each. Return every string formed by choosing one mapped letter for each input digit; the input has at most four digits.
Idea: Recursively choose each possible letter for the current digit, append it to a path, and continue until all digits are consumed.
Technique and why it applies: The answer is a Cartesian product of small letter sets; backtracking explores one branch for every possible prefix and records complete combinations.
Invariant: At recursion depth k, the path contains exactly one selected letter for each of the first k digits.
Edge cases: Although the stated constraints use at least one digit, returning an empty list for empty input is a safe convention. Digits 7 and 9 have four letters.
Complexity: Time and output space are O(4^n * n) in the worst case because there can be 4^n strings of length n.
space_complexity: O(4^n * n) for output; O(n) recursion/path
complexity_reason: Each complete combination has n characters and at most 4^n combinations are produced.

title: 4Sum
approach_name: Sort, fix two values, sweep two pointers
notes:
Task and constraints: Return unique quadruplets using four distinct indices whose values sum to target. Values can be as large as one billion in magnitude, so sum arithmetic must be wide enough in Java.
Idea: Sort, fix the first two indices, then sweep the remaining interval with left and right pointers. Skip duplicates at every chosen position.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting makes the sum monotonic as either pointer moves and makes equal values adjacent, allowing unique quadruplets without a set.
Invariant: For each fixed pair, the active pointer interval contains all not-yet-excluded candidate pairs that could match target.
Edge cases: Arrays shorter than four return an empty list. Java must promote the first operand to long before adding four values to avoid overflow.
Complexity: Time is O(n^3) after sorting. Extra space is O(log n) typical sort stack space, excluding output.
space_complexity: O(log n) typical sort stack, excluding output
complexity_reason: Two fixed-index loops each use a linear two-pointer scan.

title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
approach_name: Fast and slow pointers with dummy head
notes:
Task and constraints: Remove the nth node from the end of a singly linked list. The list has at least one node and n is guaranteed to be within its length.
Idea: Place fast and slow pointers at a dummy node, advance fast by n nodes, then advance both until fast reaches the tail. Remove slow.next.
Technique and why it applies: The fixed gap of n nodes means that when fast reaches the last node, slow is positioned immediately before the target node.
Invariant: After the initial gap is established, fast remains n nodes ahead of slow as both move through the list.
Edge cases: A dummy node makes removing the head work the same as removing any other node. n may equal the full list length.
Complexity: Time is O(L) because the pointers traverse the list once. Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Two pointers and one dummy node are the only extra structures.

title: Valid Parentheses
notes:
Task and constraints: The input contains only bracket characters. Every opener must be matched by the same bracket type in the correct nested order, and every closer must have a preceding unmatched opener.
Idea: Push the expected closing bracket for each opener. For each closer, fail if the stack is empty or its top is not that closer; at the end, the stack must be empty.
Technique and why it applies: Bracket nesting is last-in, first-out: the most recently opened bracket must be the first one closed.
Invariant: The stack holds exactly the closing brackets expected for all currently unmatched opening brackets, in the order they must appear.
Edge cases: A closer at the beginning fails immediately; a leftover opener makes the final stack non-empty. Empty input would be valid under the rule, although the stated constraint excludes it.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each character is processed once. Extra space is O(n) for the stack in the worst case.
complexity_reason: Each bracket is pushed and popped at most once.
